facts.fact: Dragon-like steel struts steady the 2,000 m² turf-covered roof against hurricane winds.

facts.fact: Every room has daylight except the 800 m² hall, whose movable west wall can open it to the amphitheatre and lobby.

facts.fact: A tall cast-in-place concrete wall in the main hall is the main bearing element; everything rests on it or relates to it.

facts.fact: The long steel spans from this wall make room in the lobby for flowing, snake-like stairs and a ramp.

facts.fact: The lobby and ramps are in Norwegian slate, and the wood floors are Swedish pine.

facts.quote: St. Hallvard's monastery and church in Oslo, designed by the architects Lund & Slaatto, has three sections: the monastery, parish offices, and the church, surrounding a circular central nave.

facts.fact: The Ningbo Museum of Art (2005) is one of Wang Shu's major projects.

facts.fact: The historic Clock Tower stands between the centre and the Star Ferry pier.

facts.quote: The center was designed in 2011 by the Spanish architecture team MADE IN Architects, a group created specifically for this competition and led by architect Manuel Monteserin.

facts.quote: It comprises an outdoor amphitheater for 10,000 people, a concert hall for 6,000 people, six live houses known as the "Whales," five restaurants connected by an elevated walkway, two towers containing offices, museum spaces, and rehearsal rooms, an exhibition center, and a network of parks and promenades that link the entire site.

facts.fact: The live houses' green roofs form walkable hills over the harbour.

facts.fact: Its name means 'Farming Ch'an', because its early residents practised Ch'an and grew their own food.
facts.quote: It's named ' Farming Ch'an ' as its early residents dedicated themselves to Ch'an practice and grew their own food.

facts.quote: The library was designed by the Rotterdam-based architectural firm MVRDV along with the Tianjin Urban Planning and Design Institute (TUPDI), a group of local architects.

facts.fact: At 126 m, the Prime Tower was Switzerland's tallest building from 2011 until 2015.

facts.fact: The Kirchner Museum Davos is devoted to the life and work of the Expressionist Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, who lived in Davos from 1918 to 1938.

facts.fact: The new building, donated by Kirchner's estate administrator Roman Norbert Ketterer, opened on 4 September 1992.
facts.quote: On September 4, 1992, a new building, donated by Kirchner's estate administrator, Roman Norbert Ketterer, was opened.

facts.fact: It was Annette Gigon and Mike Guyer's first major commission.

facts.fact: It is seen as a pioneering example of a new approach to museum architecture.

facts.fact: It received the Velux Foundation's Daylight Award in 2012.
facts.quote: In 2012 it received the Daylight Award from the Velux Foundation, founded in 1980, the most valuable architecture prize in Switzerland.

facts.fact: Drawing on Davos's climate, light and flat-roofed buildings, the architects made four cubes as exhibition halls.
facts.quote: Based on the regional conditions (climate and light conditions, Davos flat roof architecture), but above all with the idea of an ideal encounter between the visitors and works of art, the architects designed four cubes as exhibition halls.

facts.fact: A branching foyer with wide windows links the cubes and opens views to the Alpine landscape.
facts.quote: They are connected by a branched foyer with wide window fronts, which is meant as a place for reflection, and at the same time opens up a view of the alpine landscape that was si inspirational for Kirchner.

facts.fact: The facade is clad entirely in glass, opaque and clear panels alternating, and the roof is covered with broken glass.

facts.fact: The German Maritime Museum in Bremerhaven opened its main building on 5 September 1975.

facts.quote: Some of his most important buildings were only finished after his 1972 death in Berlin, including the German Maritime Museum in  Bremerhaven, the theatre in Wolfsburg and the Berlin State Library.

facts.fact: The museum is Scharoun's building plus museum ships in Bremerhaven's Old Harbour.
facts.quote: The museum consists of the building planned by Hans Scharoun as well as several museum ships in the Old Harbour of Bremerhaven, including the Seute Deern windjammer.

facts.fact: The building and its fleet of eight ships were listed as a heritage ensemble in 2005.
facts.quote: The building and the 8 ships of the museum fleet, located between the Old Harbor and the Weser dike, as an ensemble, were placed under Bremen Cultural heritage management in 2005.

facts.fact: It collects, researches and presents German maritime history.

facts.fact: A cog built around 1380 and found in the Weser in 1962 went on show in 2000 after long conservation.

facts.fact: The buildings were restored in 2024.

facts.fact: The Kunstmuseum Basel holds the oldest public art collection in the world and is generally seen as Switzerland's most important art museum.

facts.fact: A competition with five Pritzker laureates among the entrants was won by the young local firm Christ & Gantenbein.

facts.fact: The new building is angled, faced with concrete bricks and kept to the height of the original museum.

facts.fact: The extension adds 2,750 m² of galleries, bringing the total to nearly 10,000 m².

facts.quote: The original museum now houses art from the 15th century to 1950, with later works in the extension.

facts.fact: The Museum Brandhorst opened in Munich on 21 May 2009 to show the modern art collection of Udo and Anette Brandhorst.

facts.fact: Sauerbruch Hutton designed a long, two-storey rectangular building next to the Pinakothek der Moderne in the Kunstareal.

facts.fact: It was nominated for the Stirling Prize and the EU Prize for Contemporary Architecture.

facts.fact: The Wiener Stadthalle is a multi-purpose indoor arena and convention centre in Vienna's 15th district.
facts.quote: Wiener Stadthalle (German: [ˈviːnɐ ˈʃtathalə]; English: Viennese City Hall) is a multi-purpose indoor arena and convention center located in the 15th district of Vienna, Austria.

facts.quote: The Austrian architect Roland Rainer designed the original halls, which were constructed between 1953 and 1958 and later expanded in 1974, 1994 and 2006.

facts.fact: Its main hall is Austria's largest indoor arena, holding up to about 16,083 people.

facts.fact: With them Lamela brought 'suspended architecture' to Spain, using high-strength post-tensioned concrete instead of steel.

facts.fact: When built they held the world record for suspended slabs, 21, using pre-stressed concrete.

facts.fact: A 2020–2024 renovation replaced the Art Deco 'plug' crown with a four-storey structure over both towers.

facts.fact: The building won the Spanish Architecture Award and a FAD Award in 2017.
facts.quote: The museum building received two main awards: The Spanish Architecture Award (2017). The FAD Awards for Architecture and Interior Design (2017).

facts.fact: Cruz y Ortiz, the Seville studio of Antonio Cruz Villalón and Antonio Ortiz García, designed Santa Justa Station in Seville between 1987 and 1992.
facts.quote: 1987–1992 Santa Justa Train Station, Seville. Spain

facts.fact: The station won the Brunel 92 International Award for Railway Design in 1992.
facts.quote: 1992 Brunel 92 International Award for Railway Design for the Santa Justa Train Station in Seville.

facts.fact: It was a finalist for the Mies van der Rohe Award for European Architecture in 1992.
facts.quote: 1992 Finalists in Mies van der Rohe Pavilion Award for European Architecture for the Santa Justa Train Station in Seville

facts.fact: It won the Spanish Architecture Award in 1993.
facts.quote: 1993 Spanish Architecture Award for the Santa Justa Station in Seville, granted by the Governing Council of the Professional Colleges of Architects of Spain and the Ministry of Public Works, Transport and Environment.

facts.fact: La Ricarda is a house in El Prat de Llobregat by Antoni Bonet i Castellana, between the airport's runways and the sea, and is now a museum; Emilio Bofill's firm built it.
facts.quote: Among the projects he built, one that stands out is the house known as La Ricarda in El Prat de Llobregat, by Antoni Bonet i Castellana, between the airport's runways and the sea, now a museum.

facts.fact: The house was built between 1948 and 1963.
facts.quote: La Ricarda House in El Prat de Llobregat (1948–1963)

facts.fact: The Pavilhão do Conhecimento is one of the buildings left from Expo '98 in Lisbon, with the Pavilhão Atlântico and the Oceanário.
facts.quote: Lisbon: Expo '98 was divided into several structures: Pavilhão Atlântico, Casino Lisboa, Oceanário and Pavilhão do Conhecimento.

facts.fact: The painter Nadir Afonso gave his own collection to a foundation in his name and engaged Álvaro Siza to design its headquarters in his home town of Chaves.
facts.quote: He formed a foundation bearing his name, to which he donated his personal artwork collection, and engaged Pritzker Prize-winner architect Álvaro Siza to design its headquarters in his hometown of Chaves.

facts.fact: The Metropolitano is a football stadium in the San Blas-Canillejas district of Madrid, home of Atlético Madrid since 2017.
facts.quote: The Metropolitano Stadium (Spanish: Estadio Metropolitano), officially referred to as Riyadh Air Metropolitano Stadium due to sponsorship, is a football stadium in Madrid, located in the Rosas neighbourhood in the San Blas-Canillejas district. It has been the home stadium of Atlético Madrid since 2017.

facts.fact: The first stadium on the site, begun in 1990, was designed by Cruz y Ortiz.
facts.quote: Construction of the new stadium began in 1990 and was based on a design proposed by Cruz y Ortiz.

facts.fact: Its single 20,000-seat tier earned it the nickname La Peineta (the comb), for its likeness to a traditional hair comb.
facts.quote: The single seating tier stadium with a capacity of 20,000 seats became known as La Peineta (the comb) because of its similarity with a traditional hair comb.

facts.fact: Rebuilt for Atlético, it reopened on 16 September 2017 with a match against Málaga.
facts.quote: The stadium was rebuilt and the new facility was reopened to the public on 16 September 2017, when Atlético Madrid faced Málaga in La Liga.

facts.fact: The rebuilding raised its capacity from 20,000 to 68,456 seats.
facts.quote: The stadium had a capacity of 20,000 spectators upon its closure and re-opened with a seating capacity of 68,456 after it was rebuilt.

facts.fact: The name Metropolitano recalls the 1923–1966 ground where Atlético played before the Vicente Calderón.
facts.quote: On 9 December 2016, the club announced that the renovated stadium's official name would be Wanda Metropolitano – Wanda for sponsorship reasons and Metropolitano after the 1923–1966 arena which hosted Atlético's matches before Vicente Calderón.

facts.fact: It was the world's first stadium lit entirely by LEDs.
facts.quote: The stadium was also the first 100% LED stadium in the world.

facts.fact: It hosted the 2019 UEFA Champions League Final, in which Liverpool beat Tottenham Hotspur.
facts.quote: On 1 June 2019, the stadium hosted the 2019 UEFA Champions League Final between Tottenham Hotspur and Liverpool, in which Liverpool defeated Spurs 2–0.

facts.fact: Grosvenor Place is an office tower on George Street, Sydney, designed by Harry Seidler.
facts.quote: Grosvenor Place is a commercial office tower in George Street, Sydney, Australia, which was designed by renowned architect Harry Seidler.

facts.fact: It stands at the edge of The Rocks and is 180 metres tall with 44 floors.
facts.quote: The building provides office space on the south-eastern edge of the city centre suburb of The Rocks, adjacent to the northern limits of Sydney's CBD; it is 180 metres tall and contains 44 floors.

facts.fact: The complex fills a whole block and keeps two low heritage buildings, the Johnsons Building and Royal Naval House, with a diagonal walkway between them and the tower.
facts.quote: As well as the modernist office tower facing George Street, the complex includes the Johnsons Building and Royal Naval House – two low-set heritage significant buildings in Grosvenor Street. There is a diagonal path for pedestrians, which runs between the heritage buildings and the main tower.

facts.fact: Each floor is a column-free plate of 2,000 square metres, so a tenant can take a whole open level.
facts.quote: This mandate was realised through the design of a large, open floor design; incorporating column-free floor plates, each floor spanning 2,000 square metres (22,000 square feet).

facts.fact: The plan is two crescents around an elliptical core, turned to catch views of the harbour, the Harbour Bridge and the Opera House.
facts.quote: The form of the tower features two crescents with an elliptical central core. The positioning and orientation of Grosvenor Place's two quadrants was chosen to maximise views over Sydney Harbour, Sydney Harbour Bridge and Sydney Opera House down George Street.

facts.fact: It is built of a concrete core with steel beams and prefabricated granite facades.
facts.quote: Structurally the building consists of a concrete core with steel beams and prefabricated granite facades.

facts.fact: It won the RAIA Lustig & Moar National Prize in 1989 and the Sulman Award in 1991.
facts.quote: In 1989, Grosvenor Place won the RAIA Lustig & Moar National Prize and the 1991 Sulman Award.

facts.fact: The lobby holds Pillars & Cones, an artwork by the American minimalist Frank Stella.
facts.quote: Grosvenor Place's lobby contains Pillars & Cones, an artwork by American minimalist, Frank Stella.

facts.fact: QV1 is a 40-storey, 163-metre modernist office tower in Perth, completed in 1991.
facts.quote: QV1 is a 40-storey modernist skyscraper in Perth, Western Australia. Completed in 1991, the 163-metre (535 ft) building is the fourth-tallest building in Perth, after Central Park, Brookfield Place and 108 St Georges Terrace.

facts.fact: Its name comes from the Latin phrase Quo vadis, 'where are you going?'.
facts.quote: The tower was named "Q.V.1" after the Latin phrase Quo vadis (meaning "where are you going?").

facts.fact: Seidler gave the tower a narrow profile towards Parliament House to lessen its impact in the Parliamentary Precinct.
facts.quote: According to architect Harry Seidler, one of the architectural objectives in the design of QV1 was to minimise the impact of the tower when viewed from Parliament House, and this was addressed by offering a narrow profile to that direction.

facts.fact: Passive design cuts energy use: tinted double glazing with horizontal and vertical sunshades beside the windows.
facts.quote: Another of the design briefs identified by Harry Seidler was that the building should employ passive design in order to minimise energy costs. This is achieved through the use of tinted double glazed windows, as well as the installation alongside windows of horizontal and vertical sun shades.

facts.fact: A reinforced concrete core, 21.5 metres square, takes the wind loads.
facts.quote: The tower has a reinforced concrete core, measuring 21.5 metres (71 ft) on each side, which bears lateral forces including wind loading.

facts.fact: Perimeter concrete columns 7.3 metres apart leave the floors free of internal columns.
facts.quote: The perimeter of the building features reinforced concrete support columns spaced 7.3 metres (24 ft) apart, and there are no internal columns within floors.

facts.fact: At the St Georges Terrace entrance, stone-clad hyperboloid supports carry two perimeter columns that stop above them at the third floor.
facts.quote: The main entrance to QV1 from St Georges Terrace features a set of stone-clad hyperboloid supports that carry the loads of the two perimeter columns which terminate above them on the third floor.

facts.fact: It won the Richard Roach Jewell Award for Enduring Architecture in 2019.
facts.quote: 2019 Richard Roach Jewell Award for Enduring Architecture

facts.fact: Featherston House in Ivanhoe, Victoria, was designed by Robin Boyd of Romberg & Boyd in 1967 and completed in 1969.
facts.quote: Featherston House is in Ivanhoe, Victoria. It was designed by leading Australian architect Robin Boyd of Romberg & Boyd in 1967. The house was completed in 1969.

facts.fact: It sits on sloping ground at the edge of a suburban parkland.
facts.quote: The Featherston House sits on sloping ground, at the edge of a parkland in the suburbs.

facts.fact: The owners gave Boyd freedom to design around the theme of living in a garden.
facts.quote: The Featherston's, owners of the house, were open to new ideas and Boyd had the creative freedom to design an alternative scheme, with the theme of living in a garden.

facts.fact: Full glass walls look onto the bush, the garden is on the ground floor and platforms project from a central chimney, like a tree house.
facts.quote: The design approach was considered radical at that time with full glassed windows, overlooking the bush land, its garden at the ground floor and platforms that are placed strategically from the chimney, placed in the centre. The Featherston house took on the idea of a beautiful tree house.

facts.fact: The roof is translucent cellular polycarbonate, letting soft light into the space below all day.
facts.quote: The roof is translucent cellular polycarbonate, allowing soft light to pass through and light up  the space below at all times of the day.

facts.fact: A glass wall on the south side brings in more light and views of the treed parkland.
facts.quote: A wall of glass at the south elevation of the house lets additional light in and also provides views to the treed parkland beyond.

facts.fact: Three flaps built into the platform draw air from a 'cool room' to ventilate the house.
facts.quote: The design includes three flaps built into the platform which can be utilised to draw air from a “cool room" to ventilate the house.

facts.fact: Harry Seidler designed the Riverside Centre in Brisbane between 1983 and 1986.
facts.quote: 1983–86: Riverside Centre, Brisbane

facts.fact: Seidler worked with Mario Desideri, Pier Luigi Nervi's successor, on the Riverside Centre.
facts.quote: Seidler later worked with Nervi's successor Mario Desideri for the Riverside Centre in Brisbane.

facts.fact: On towers such as Riverside Centre, Seidler answered the Australian climate with concrete, sunshades and shaped rain canopies.
facts.quote: Thus, later in his career, he sought to use more thermally stable materials like reinforced concrete and to respond to the Australian climate by the extensive use of sunshades and flamboyantly-shaped rain protecting canopies on his skyscrapers, (such as Grosvenor Place, Riverside Centre, and QV1), large covered balconies in his houses, as well as shaping his designs to maximize views and enjoyment of the outdoors from inside.

facts.fact: It won the Robin Gibson Award for Enduring Architecture in 2011.
facts.quote: 2011 Robin Gibson Award for Enduring Architecture, Riverside Centre, Brisbane

facts.fact: Kenneth Frampton wrote a book on it, Riverside Centre, Harry Seidler (1988).
facts.quote: Frampton, Kenneth (1988). Riverside Centre, Harry Seidler.

facts.fact: The Queen Elizabeth II Courts of Law, also called the Brisbane Supreme and District Court, stands at 415 George Street, Brisbane.
facts.quote: The Queen Elizabeth II Courts of Law, also referred to as the Brisbane Supreme and District Court, is a court building located at 415 George Street in Brisbane, Queensland, Australia.

facts.fact: Completed in 2012 for the Supreme and District Courts of Queensland, it forms a legal precinct filling a whole city block with the neighbouring Magistrates Court.
facts.quote: Completed in 2012 as a purpose-built building for the Supreme Court of Queensland and the District Court of Queensland, the building together with the adjacent Brisbane Magistrates Court building created a legal precinct in Brisbane, which occupies an entire city block between George Street, Roma Street and Turbot Street.

facts.fact: It is one of Australia's largest court buildings, with 39 courtrooms, a ceremonial court, the Supreme Court Library and rooms for 68 judges.
facts.quote: It is one of the largest court buildings in Australia and includes 39 courtrooms, 1 large ceremonial court, Queensland Court of Appeal, 23 criminal courts and 14 civil courts, the Supreme Court Library, accommodation for 68 judges and a cell block in the basement.

facts.fact: The building has better facilities for victims of crime, witnesses, judges, lawyers and the public.
facts.quote: The complex, shared between both courts, features enhanced facilities for victims of crime, witnesses, judges, lawyers and members of the public.

facts.fact: The Supreme Court foyer holds the Sir Harry Gibbs Legal Heritage Centre, a museum of Queensland's legal history.
facts.quote: The foyer of the Supreme Court also hosts the Sir Harry Gibbs Legal Heritage Centre, a museum dedicated to Queensland's legal history.

facts.fact: It was named after Queen Elizabeth II to mark her Diamond Jubilee.
facts.quote: The complex was named in the honour of Queen Elizabeth II to mark her Diamond Jubilee.

facts.fact: The RMIT Design Hub holds research, archive, exhibition and studio space for RMIT University on the old Carlton & United Breweries site in Melbourne.
facts.quote: The RMIT Design Hub is a research, archive, exhibition, and studio space of the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology in Melbourne, Australia located on the historic Carlton & United Breweries site.

facts.fact: Completed in May 2012, it was designed by Sean Godsell Architects with Peddle Thorp Architects.
facts.quote: Completed in May 2012, the Design Hub was designed by Sean Godsell Architects in association with Peddle Thorp Architects.

facts.fact: Its sandblasted glass discs form a second skin that controls sun, turned by motors that a computer sets to Melbourne's daily weather.
facts.quote: With the current material of sandblasted glass, the disks operate as a 'second skin' controlling solar gain and access. An internal computer controls this facade by adjusting each cell with rotational motors, according to Melbourne's daily weather.

facts.fact: The glass discs on steel cylinders were inspired by the brewery that once ran on the site.
facts.quote: Inspiration for the lucid discs with its steel cylindrical structure came from the beer business that once ran on the CUB Brewery site.

facts.fact: The shade cells can be swapped for solar cells as solar technology improves.
facts.quote: The shade cells have been designed so that they can be easily replaced with solar cells as research into solar energy results in improved technology and the infrastructure for that evolution has been built into the façade and building management systems.

facts.fact: It is two buildings around a central forecourt: one for research and archives, one for exhibitions and work spaces.
facts.quote: The Design Hub consists of two buildings with a central forecourt in between. One building is for research and archives and the other is for exhibitions and working spaces.

facts.fact: Inside, galvanised steel walkway grating clads the walls, recalling RMIT's industrial roots.
facts.quote: Influences that addressed the choice in materials of the interior, include RMIT being an industrial college, which is reflected in the use of galvanized steel industrial walkway grating as a cladding material on the walls, creating an industrial atmosphere.

facts.fact: It won the Victorian Architecture Medal in 2013.
facts.quote: 2013 The Victorian Architecture Medal - Australian Institute of Architects Victorian Chapter

facts.fact: The Swanston Academic Building is an RMIT University building on Swanston Street, Melbourne, designed by the firm Lyons.
facts.quote: The Swanston Academic building is an RMIT building designed by the architecture firm Lyons and is located on Swanston Street in Melbourne across from Peter Corrigan designed building 8 and ARM's Storey Hall.

facts.fact: It was built between September 2010 and September 2012.
facts.quote: Construction began in September 2010 and was completed in September 2012.

facts.fact: It has 35,000 square metres of floor space over 11 storeys, including six large lecture theatres.
facts.quote: The new building contains 35,000 square metres (380,000 sq ft) of floor space, is 11 storeys high (including basement) and provides 6 large lecture theatres for students.

facts.fact: Its colourful facade is meant to reflect the city around it, to 'wear the cloak of the city'.
facts.quote: The colourful building is intended to reflect the cities surroundings in the façade. “The idea is to wear the ‘cloak’ of the city”.

facts.fact: The colours were taken from a survey of Melbourne's main colours.
facts.quote: Predominant colours of Melbourne were derived from a survey, which has been reflected in the colour palette of the SAB.

facts.fact: Lyons mapped lines from the site to Melbourne's landmark buildings and fed them into a computer algorithm that generated the building's form.
facts.quote: The process involved mapping lines from the site to these buildings. Using these lines we then created a computerized algorithm that generated the three-dimensional shapes and form of the building.

facts.fact: The best viewpoints became student 'portals' on each level, linking activity inside to the cityscape.
facts.quote: The best viewpoints then became the location for the student ‘portals’ on each level that connect student activities inside the building with the surrounding cityscape.

facts.fact: External panels and triangular elements shade the facade to different degrees depending on orientation.
facts.quote: Façade is composed of external panels and triangular elements, which provide different degrees of shading, based on the orientation of the building.

facts.fact: The Melbourne School of Design building at the University of Melbourne's Parkville campus is named after vice-chancellor Glyn Davis.
facts.quote: There are buildings named after him on the campus of Griffith University at Nathan (named Glyn Davis Building in 2010), and the Melbourne School of Design at the University of Melbourne Parkville, opened in 2010.

facts.fact: Nonda Katsalidis designed the Ian Potter Museum of Art at the University of Melbourne in 1998, under the firm Nation Fender Katsalidis.
facts.quote: Ian Potter Museum of Art, University of Melbourne (1998) (Nation Fender Katsalidis)

facts.fact: The museum is in Carlton, Melbourne.
facts.quote: Ian Potter Museum of Art (1998), Carlton

facts.fact: It won the RAIA Victorian Architecture Medal, the Melbourne Prize and the William Wardell Award.
facts.quote: 1999 – RAIA Victorian Architecture Medal, Melbourne Prize and William Wardell Award (for the Ian Potter Museum of Art)

facts.fact: Wellington Central Library (Te Matapihi ki te Ao Nui) is the city's public library, owned by Wellington City Council and listed as a Category 1 historic place.
facts.quote: Wellington Central Library (Māori: Te Matapihi ki te Ao Nui) is a public library building in the central business district of Wellington, in New Zealand. It is owned by Wellington City Council and is listed as a Category 1 historic place by Heritage New Zealand.

facts.fact: Athfield Architects were commissioned to design it in 1989.
facts.quote: In 1989, Athfield Architects were commissioned to design a new Wellington Central Library.

facts.fact: Ian Athfield visited libraries in the United States and took up the idea of a library as an 'information supermarket'.
facts.quote: Ian Athfield visited libraries in the United States and became interested in the vision of a library as an "information supermarket", providing as much information as possible to as many people as possible.

facts.fact: The three library floors facing Civic Square sit behind a curved glass wall lined with window seats and desks.
facts.quote: The curved wall of the three storeys of the library facing Civic Square was made of glass with window seats and desks looking into the square.

facts.fact: A colonnade of metal nikau palms runs from Victoria Street up a ramp to Civic Square.
facts.quote: A colonnade ran along the outside of the building from Victoria Street up a ramp to Civic Square, with its columns designed as metal nikau palms.

facts.fact: It was said to be the first public library in Australasia with a café inside.
facts.quote: The library was said to be the first public library in Australasia to have a café inside it, though the café had separate entrances for security reasons.

facts.fact: Heritage New Zealand calls it an excellent example of late 20th-century library design and postmodern architecture in New Zealand.
facts.quote: Heritage New Zealand states that Wellington Central Library has significance as an excellent example of late twentieth century library design and postmodern architecture in New Zealand.

facts.fact: It closed in March 2019 over earthquake concerns and reopened in March 2026 after redesign and strengthening.
facts.quote: The building was closed to the public at short notice on 19 March 2019, after Wellington City Council was advised by engineers that the building had structural vulnerabilities which meant it might not perform well in the event of a significant earthquake. Redesign and restructuring works were completed by September 2025 and the building was re-opened to the public in March 2026.

facts.fact: The Palmerston North City Library is the city's main public library, run by Palmerston North City Council.
facts.quote: The Palmerston North City Library is the main public library provided by the Palmerston North City Council for the residents of Palmerston North, New Zealand.

facts.fact: It occupies the restored and extended C M Ross building on The Square, designed by Ian Athfield and opened in 1996.
facts.quote: The Palmerston North City Library is located in The Square in the restored and extended C M Ross building. The design for the building was created by New Zealand architect Ian Athfield and was opened in 1996.

facts.fact: The library is branded 'The Living Room of the City'.
facts.quote: The Palmerston North City Library is branded as "The Living Room of the City" and exists "To inspire people to explore the pathways of the world – Te Ara Whanui o Te Ao".

facts.fact: The central library, in its sixth home, occupies the former D.I.C. department store building.
facts.quote: The library has occupied a number of buildings over the years and the current central library is the 6th location, now occupying the former D.I.C. department store building.

facts.fact: The former D.I.C. building was registered as a Category II heritage building in 1982.
facts.quote: The former D.I.C. building was registered by the New Zealand Historic Places Trust (since renamed to Heritage New Zealand) on 2 July 1982 as a Category II heritage building with registration number 1256.

facts.fact: The building on The Square is award-winning.
facts.quote: It provides recreational and educational opportunities from an award-winning building located on The Square in the centre of the City, as well as four other branch libraries around the City.

facts.fact: Melbourne Recital Centre is a venue and organisation for live music in Melbourne.
facts.quote: Melbourne Recital Centre (MRC) is a venue and organisation for live music in Melbourne, Victoria, Australia.

facts.fact: It opened in 2009 as part of a complex with the Melbourne Theatre Company's Southbank Theatre, designed by Ashton Raggatt McDougall with acoustics by Arup.
facts.quote: The building was opened in 2009, as part of the Melbourne Recital Centre and Melbourne Theatre Company Southbank Theatre complex designed by Ashton Raggat McDougall, with acoustic and theatre consulting by Arup.

facts.fact: It is Melbourne's second largest classical music hall, after Hamer Hall.
facts.quote: It is Melbourne's second largest auditorium for classical music (after Hamer Hall in Arts Centre Melbourne).

facts.fact: Its main hall, the Elisabeth Murdoch Hall, is a 'modified shoe box' with 1,000 seats on two levels; a smaller Salon sits beside it.
facts.quote: The centre features two auditoria, the Elisabeth Murdoch Hall, and a smaller Salon. The former, a "modified shoe box" shaped music venue, is named after Dame Elisabeth Murdoch. It has seating for 1000 on two levels.

facts.fact: To keep out traffic and tram noise, the hall is wrapped in 250 mm of concrete set on 38 steel springs.
facts.quote: To eliminate noise from the nearby Southbank Boulevard cars and trams, it is surrounded by 250mm of concrete, mounted on 38 steel springs.

facts.fact: The interior is lined in hoop pine plywood, tuned for the bass of cellos and low brass.
facts.quote: The interior is lined with Hoop Pine plywood and is designed to give ideal bass response for cello and low brass.

facts.fact: The shoebox shape, size and timber surfaces give a reverberation time of 1.6 to 1.8 seconds.
facts.quote: The shoebox shape, size and wooden surfaces were designed to provide a reverberation time of 1.6 to 1.8 seconds

facts.fact: The complex won the Victorian Architecture Medal in 2009.
facts.quote: The complex also won the Victorian Architecture Medal, the William Wardell Award for Public Architecture and the Joseph Reed Award for Urban Design at the Australian Institute of Architects Victoria Chapter State Architecture Awards in 2009.

facts.fact: Melbourne Museum is a natural and cultural history museum in the Carlton Gardens, Melbourne.
facts.quote: The Melbourne Museum is a natural and cultural history museum located in the Carlton Gardens in Melbourne, Australia.

facts.fact: It is a postmodernist building designed by Denton Corker Marshall.
facts.quote: The Melbourne Museum is a post-modernist building designed by Denton Corker Marshall architects.

facts.fact: It was opened on 21 October 2000 by Victoria's premier, Steve Bracks.
facts.quote: The museum was constructed during the period of the Kennett government (1992–1999) and was opened on 21 October 2000 by the Premier of Victoria, Steve Bracks.

facts.fact: It works both as one building and as a network of separate buildings set into the Carlton Gardens landscape.
facts.quote: It is designed as both a single building and a network of individual buildings integrated into the landscape of the Carlton Gardens.

facts.fact: It lines up on an axis with the neighbouring Royal Exhibition Building and refers to it and to the city's skyscrapers.
facts.quote: The museum is axially aligned with the adjacent Italianate Royal Exhibition Building and references it, along with the skyscrapers of Melbourne's central business district.

facts.fact: Two long, high, sloping blades rise from the entrance opposite the Royal Exhibition Building and lead visitors in from the street.
facts.quote: The most prominent element of the building are the two very long, very high, sloping canopies (or blades) that rise up from the centrally placed entrance opposite the north door of the Royal Exhibition Building; each act to guide visitors from the street into the museum.

facts.fact: A blade of roof rising to 35 metres encloses a small rainforest.
facts.quote: In Australia, Denton Corker Marshall is best known for landmark buildings such as the Melbourne Museum, which features a "blade" section of roof rising to 35 metres, enclosing a small rainforest, the Melbourne Exhibition Centre, which has a roof resembling a giant aircraft wing, and the Melbourne Gateway and Bolte Bridge, both part of the CityLink project.

facts.fact: At its centre is the Forest Gallery, a living temperate forest of eastern Victoria.
facts.quote: The centrepiece of the new building houses the Forest Gallery, an exhibition portraying the temperate forests of eastern Victoria.

facts.fact: The Michael Fowler Centre is a concert hall and convention centre on reclaimed land beside Civic Square, Wellington.
facts.quote: The Michael Fowler Centre is a concert hall and convention centre in Wellington, New Zealand. It was constructed on reclaimed land next to Civic Square, and is the pre-eminent concert site in central Wellington.

facts.fact: It was first commissioned in 1975 as the New Town Hall.
facts.quote: The building was initially commissioned in 1975 as the New Town Hall, with the original intention being to demolish the Wellington Town Hall.

facts.fact: Miles Warren and Maurice Mahoney designed it, with acoustic help from Harold Marshall of the University of Auckland.
facts.quote: It was designed by architects Miles Warren and Maurice Mahoney of Warren and Mahoney, with acoustic assistance from University of Auckland researcher A. Harold Marshall.

facts.fact: Mayor Michael Fowler wanted it to outdo Christchurch Town Hall, also by Warren and Mahoney.
facts.quote: Fowler desired a building that would remove Wellington from the "doldrums" and outdo the Christchurch Town Hall, also designed by Warren and Mahoney.

facts.fact: It opened in September 1983 at a final cost of $17.5 million.
facts.quote: After delays, the building was opened in September 1983 by the Duke of Wellington, with the final cost being $17.5 million.

facts.fact: The outside mixes stainless steel cladding, concrete panels and a raised glass circulation passage; the main hall uses timber reflectors.
facts.quote: The exterior of the building is constructed of multiple materials, including stainless steel cladding, concrete panelling, and a raised glass circulation passage. The main auditorium uses wooden reflectors.

facts.fact: It received the New Zealand Institute of Architects' Enduring Architecture award in 2010.
facts.quote: It received an Enduring Architecture award from the New Zealand Institute of Architects in 2010.

facts.fact: In 2023 it was declared earthquake prone, and options including demolition were put forward.
facts.quote: In 2023 the building was marked as earthquake prone; the following year, three scenarios were proposed, including demolition and remediation.

facts.fact: The Sky Tower is a telecommunications and observation tower in Auckland.
facts.quote: The Sky Tower is a telecommunications and observation tower in Auckland, New Zealand.

facts.fact: Completed in 1997, it became a landmark of the Auckland skyline and was the tallest freestanding structure in the Southern Hemisphere from 1996 to 2022.
facts.quote: Since its completion in 1997, the Sky Tower has become an iconic landmark in Auckland's skyline, due to its height and design. It was the tallest freestanding structure in the Southern Hemisphere from 1996 to 2022.

facts.fact: It was built as part of the SkyCity casino precinct, briefed to be both a tourist attraction and a telecommunications facility.
facts.quote: The tower was constructed as a part of the Skycity casino precinct. The Skycity Entertainment Group's initial brief for the project were that they required a tower that was both a high-quality tourist attraction, and a marketable telecommunications facility.

facts.fact: Gordon Moller of Craig Craig Moller designed it, and it won a New Zealand Institute of Architects National Award.
facts.quote: It was designed by Gordon Moller of Craig Craig Moller Architects and has received a New Zealand Institute of Architects National Award as well as regional awards.

facts.fact: Built in two years and nine months, it opened on 3 August 1997.
facts.quote: Taking two years and nine months to construct, the tower opened on 3 August 1997.

facts.fact: Its 12-metre concrete shaft, holding four lifts and a stair, stands on eight 'legs' over 16 piles drilled more than 15 metres into sandstone.
facts.quote: The tower is constructed of high-performance reinforced concrete. Its 12-metre (39 ft) diameter shaft (containing four lifts and an emergency stairwell) is supported on eight "legs" based on 16 foundation piles drilled over 15 m (49 ft) deep into the local sandstone.

facts.fact: The observation decks are clad in aluminium and blue-green reflective glass.
facts.quote: The upper levels were constructed from composite materials, structural steel, precast concrete and reinforced concrete, and the observation decks clad in aluminium with blue/green reflective glass.

facts.fact: It is designed for winds over 200 km/h and to sway up to a metre in very high winds.
facts.quote: The tower is designed to withstand wind in excess of 200 km/h (120 mph) and designed to sway up to 1 metre (39 in) in excessively high winds.

facts.fact: Governor Phillip Tower is the main tower of a Sydney CBD development, completed in 1994, that includes the site of the first Government House.
facts.quote: Completed in 1994, the property development complex occupies an elevated site in the north-east area of the central business district. The complex incorporates the site of the first Government House, one of Australia's earliest and most significant sites of European heritage.

facts.fact: Denton Corker Marshall designed it, and it was seen as setting new standards of finish and design for Sydney office buildings.
facts.quote: Designed by architects Denton Corker Marshall and built by Grocon, at the time of its completion it was regarded as achieving new standards for Sydney commercial architecture in terms of finish quality and design.

facts.fact: The remains of First Government House were conserved and made part of the Museum of Sydney, built alongside.
facts.quote: Integral to the development was the conservation of the archaeological remains and their incorporation into the Museum of Sydney, which was built and opened alongside the development.

facts.fact: To keep the historic site free, the state moved its floor space to the land just behind it to the south.
facts.quote: The Government of New South Wales found a solution by transferring floor space from the area containing the historical foundation to space immediately behind to the south.

facts.fact: The tower is raised 10 floors above the street on zinc-plated transfer beams over a sandstone-clad podium, to give every level views.
facts.quote: It sits 10 floors above street level on a series of large zinc-plated transfer beams atop a 4-level sandstone-clad podium (upon which Governor Macquarie Tower also sits). This maximises views, and hence rentals, for all levels.

facts.fact: The facade is grey granite and glass; the steel-bladed roof is nicknamed 'the milk-crate'.
facts.quote: The façade is of grey granite and glass used to achieve an expensive and highly detailed finish. The steel-bladed roof features have been dubbed the milk-crate.

facts.fact: At 227 metres to the roof, it is among Sydney's tallest buildings.
facts.quote: At 227 m (745 ft), it is the seventh tallest building in the city by roof height and eleventh by architectural height, although the taller 25 Martin Place and World Tower are both only fractionally taller at 228 m (748 ft).

facts.fact: Critics have pointed to the oppressive scale of the tower at street level and an awkward relationship between the two towers.
facts.quote: Criticism of the complex has included the vast, even oppressive scale of the main tower, particularly at street level, and a perceived awkward and disjointed relationship between the two towers.

facts.fact: Tūranga is Christchurch's central public library; it opened on 12 October 2018, replacing the library closed by the 2011 earthquake.
facts.quote: Tūranga is the public library located in Central Christchurch, New Zealand. It opened on 12 October 2018 and replaced the nearby Christchurch Central Library that was closed on the day of the 2011 Christchurch earthquake.

facts.fact: A new central library was one of 17 anchor projects in the 2012 recovery plan for the city, known as the Blueprint.
facts.quote: The 2012 Christchurch Central Recovery Plan, commonly referred to as the Blueprint, identified 17 anchor projects, including a new central library.

facts.fact: It stands on the north-east corner of Cathedral Square, facing Gloucester and Colombo Streets.
facts.quote: Tūranga is located in the north-eastern quadrant of Cathedral Square and fronts Gloucester and Colombo Streets.

facts.fact: It was designed by Architectus of New Zealand and the Danish firm Schmidt Hammer Lassen.
facts.quote: The replacement library was designed by both Architectus, a New Zealand architecture firm, and Schmidt Hammer Lassen, an award-winning Danish architecture firm.

facts.fact: The design draws on the golden light on the Port Hills seen from the city.
facts.quote: The building's design is inspired by the golden hues reflected upon the Port Hills, which are an important part in Christchurch's cityscape.

facts.fact: It is a third larger than the old library and the largest library in the South Island.
facts.quote: The new library, named Tūranga, is one-third larger than the previous library, the largest library in the South Island and the third-largest in New Zealand, behind Auckland and Wellington's central libraries.

facts.fact: Its name was given by Te Ngāi Tūāhuriri rūnanga and refers to Whitireia, the Māori name for Cathedral Square.
facts.quote: The library's name was gifted by Te Ngāi Tūāhuriri rūnanga. It makes reference to Whitireia, the Te Reo name for Cathedral Square.

facts.fact: Inside is a 7-metre touch-sensitive Discovery Wall showing an interactive digital picture of Christchurch.
facts.quote: $1.2 million 7m-long touch-sensitive Discovery Wall offering an interactive digital picture of Christchurch

facts.fact: University House is the oldest residential college at the Australian National University, opened in 1954 for its staff and postgraduate students.
facts.quote: University House at the Australian National University (ANU) is the oldest residential college in ANU. It opened in 1954 for the faculty, staff, and postgraduate students of ANU.

facts.fact: It was first planned in 1947 and designed by Brian Lewis.
facts.quote: University House was first planned in 1947 and was designed by Brian Lewis.

facts.fact: The foundation stone was laid in 1949, and in 1950 it was decided the building would also hold modern art.
facts.quote: The foundation stone for the building was placed in 1949. During construction, in 1950, it was decided that the University House would also hold modern art.

facts.fact: Prince Philip opened it on 16 February 1954.
facts.quote: The building was ceremonially opened for occupancy by Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh on 16 February 1954.

facts.fact: It began on the Oxbridge college model, with seminars and a daily formal dinner in hall with the faculty.
facts.quote: In its early years, initially intended to follow the Oxbridge collegiate system, students were required to attend regular seminars and a daily formal dinner at the hall with the faculty.

facts.fact: The Great Hall is decorated by Leonard French, with Regeneration (1972) at the rostrum end and his ten-painting series The Journey (1974).
facts.quote: The hall features are by Leonard French, who decorated the western or rostrum end with Regeneration (1972) and was also commissioned to create The Journey series (1974) of ten paintings that also decorate the Hall.

facts.fact: It is heritage-listed by ANU, the Royal Australian Institute of Architects and the Australian Government.
facts.quote: University House is also listed as a heritage site by ANU, the Royal Australian Institute of Architects and the Government of Australia and is a nominee for heritage listing by the National Trust of Australia.

facts.fact: It reopened in August 2026 after extensive repairs.
facts.quote: University House reopened after extensive repairs in August 2026.

facts.fact: Orica House, formerly ICI House, is a 19-storey office building at 1 Nicholson Street, East Melbourne.
facts.quote: Orica House (formerly ICI House) is a 19-storey office building at 1 Nicholson Street, East Melbourne, in Victoria, Australia.

facts.fact: Begun in 1955 as the Australian headquarters of Imperial Chemical Industries, it was the tallest building in Australia when finished in 1958.
facts.quote: Begun in 1955 to house the headquarters of the Australian subsidiary of Imperial Chemical Industries (since spun off as an independent public company and renamed Orica), it was the tallest building in Australia upon completion in 1958.

facts.fact: It broke Melbourne's 132-foot height limit and was Australia's first International Style skyscraper.
facts.quote: It broke Melbourne's longstanding 132 ft height limit and was the first International Style skyscraper in the country.

facts.fact: Osborn McCutcheon of Bates Smart McCutcheon modelled it on American all-glass towers such as the United Nations Secretariat.
facts.quote: The building's design, by Osborn McCutcheon (of Bates Smart McCutcheon) was closely modelled on the best of corporate design being pioneered in the United States with all-glass high-rises such as the United Nations Secretariat Building.

facts.fact: It stood for progress and corporate power in post-war Melbourne and opened the way for high-rise offices in Australian cities.
facts.quote: It symbolised progress, modernity, efficiency and corporate power in post-war Melbourne, and heralded the construction of high-rise office buildings, changing the shape of Australia's major urban centres forever.

facts.fact: Soon after completion, panes of its coloured glass shattered in the summer heat and fell to the street.
facts.quote: Soon after construction, panes of the coloured glass shattered and fell to the street below due to impurities and the heat of Melbourne's summers.

facts.fact: It was added to the Victorian Heritage Register in 1990.
facts.quote: Orica House was added to the Victorian Heritage Register on 21 March 1990 for its architectural significance to the state of Victoria.

facts.fact: In 2005 it became the first post-war office building on the Australian National Heritage List.
facts.quote: On 21 September 2005, Orica House became the first post-war office building to be added to the Australian National Heritage List.

facts.fact: Qantas House is a heritage-listed office building on Hunter Street, Sydney, designed by Rudder, Littlemore & Rudder and built from 1955 to 1957; it is also called No. 1 Chifley Square.
facts.quote: Qantas House is an Australian heritage-listed office building at 68–96 Hunter Street, Sydney. It was designed by Rudder, Littlemore & Rudder and built from 1955 to 1957 by Concrete Constructions Pty Ltd. It is also known as No. 1 Chifley Square.

facts.fact: It was the first planned world headquarters of Qantas, and the aerofoil-shaped aluminium mullions of its curtain wall express the airline's forward-looking image.
facts.quote: Historically significant as the first planned world headquarters for Qantas Empire Airways, at the time Australia's only, and Government-owned, international airline, the building, and in particular the aerofoil-shaped aluminium mullions of its curtain wall, gives form to Qantas' forward looking and expansive image at a time when air travel was taking off.

facts.fact: Prime Minister Robert Menzies opened it on 28 October 1957.
facts.quote: The building was opened by Prime Minister Robert Menzies on 28 October 1957.

facts.fact: Its segmented curved facade is a 46-metre double-glazed curtain wall of green glass with blue-green enamelled steel spandrels.
facts.quote: Qantas House is distinguished by its graceful, segmented, curved facade which consists of a 46m high, double glazed curtain wall of green glass with enamelled blue-green steel spandrel panels.

facts.fact: The curved plan follows the semicircle planned for the north side of Chifley Square in 1908.
facts.quote: In following the curve of Chifley Square, the building's plan respects the semi-circular form which was proposed for the northern side of the square in its original design of 1908.

facts.fact: It was the first office building to use Australian black granite from Adelong and green granite from near Yass.
facts.quote: Qantas House was the first office building to use Australian black granite from Adelong and Bookharn green granite from the Yass area.

facts.fact: The service cores sit against the side boundaries, which leaves room for a light well at the back.
facts.quote: However, the planning is noteworthy in that the service cores are asymmetrically placed adjacent to the boundaries with the adjoining buildings. This allows for the inclusion of a light well at the rear of the building, ensuring the penetration of light deep into the interior.

facts.fact: In 1959 the RIBA judged it the best new building in the British Commonwealth and gave it the Bronze medal.
facts.quote: Qantas House was judged the best new building in the British Commonwealth by the Royal Institute of British Architects in 1959, and was awarded the Bronze medal.

facts.fact: Bunning and Madden's most notable commission was the National Library of Australia.
facts.quote: The firm's most notable commission was the design of the National Library of Australia and the firm was most prominent between 1955 and 1970s.

facts.fact: The National Capital Development Commission commissioned the firm to design the library in 1961, with Noel Potter as project architect.
facts.quote: In 1961 the firm was commissioned to design the National Library of Australia by the National Capital Development Commission, Potter was the project architect on the National Library and finally opened Bunning and Madden's permanent office in Civic in 1964, and remained the firm's partner in charge in Canberra until retiring in 1996.

facts.fact: It is the most famous work of Walter Bunning's firm and stands in Canberra.
facts.quote: The firm's most famous work was the National Library of Australia in Canberra.

facts.fact: Eureka Tower is a 297-metre skyscraper in Southbank, Melbourne.
facts.quote: Eureka Tower is a 297.3 m (975 ft) skyscraper located in the Southbank precinct of Melbourne, Victoria, Australia.

facts.fact: It was designed by Fender Katsalidis Architects and built by Grocon.
facts.quote: The project was designed by Melbourne architectural firm Fender Katsalidis Architects and was built by Grocon (Grollo Australia).

facts.fact: It was officially opened on 11 October 2006.
facts.quote: The plaza was finished in June 2006 and the building was officially opened on 11 October 2006.

facts.fact: It is named after the 1854 Eureka Stockade rebellion: the gold crown stands for the gold rush and a red stripe for the blood spilt in the revolt.
facts.quote: Eureka Tower is named after the Eureka Stockade, a rebellion during the Victorian gold rush in 1854. This has been incorporated into the design, with the building's gold crown representing the gold rush and a red stripe representing the blood spilt during the revolt.

facts.fact: Its blue glass and white lines recall the Eureka Stockade flag.
facts.quote: The blue glass cladding that covers most of the building represents the blue background of the stockade's flag and the white lines also represent the Eureka Stockade flag.

facts.fact: The top 10 floors have glass windows plated with 24-carat gold.
facts.quote: Eureka Tower has 24 carat (99.9%) gold plated glass windows on the top 10 floors of the building.

facts.fact: When completed it was the world's tallest residential building, by roof height or highest habitable floor.
facts.quote: When measured either by the height of its roof, or by the height of its highest habitable floor, Eureka Tower was the tallest residential building in the world when completed.

facts.fact: Pumps move water between two 300,000-litre tanks at the top to damp the tower's sway in the wind.
facts.quote: A system of pumps constantly moves water between the two 300,000-litre tanks to counteract wind-induced oscillations.

facts.fact: Rialto Towers is a skyscraper complex at 525 Collins Street, Melbourne, and was the tallest office building in the Southern Hemisphere when built.
facts.quote: Rialto Towers (also called The Rialto or Rialto) is a skyscraper complex at 525 Collins Street, on the western side of the Melbourne central business district, Victoria, Australia. It was the tallest office building in the Southern Hemisphere when built.

facts.fact: Designed by Gerard de Preu and Partners with Perrott Lyon Mathieson, it was built from 1982 to 1986 and opened in October 1986.
facts.quote: Designed by architects Gerard de Preu and Partners in association with Perrott Lyon Mathieson, the building was built between 1982 and 1986, opening in October 1986.

facts.fact: Its mirrored blue-tinted glass curtain wall changes colour through the day, from dark blue to gold at sunset.
facts.quote: The massive glass curtain wall façade of reinforced blue tinted mirrored glass is its central feature and changes colour during the day, ranging from a trademark dark blue to a brilliant gold during sunset.

facts.fact: It is 251 metres high with 55 floors, made of two joined towers; the shorter North Tower has 43 floors.
facts.quote: It is 251 m (823 ft) high, with 55 floors and 3 basement floors. It comprises two conjoined towers, the shorter North Tower being 185 m (607 ft) high with 43 floors.

facts.fact: It was Australia's tallest building from 1986 until 1991.
facts.quote: When completed in 1986, The Rialto surpassed Sydney's MLC Centre to become Australia's tallest building at 251 m (823 ft). It was the tallest for five years until being surpassed by 101 Collins Street in 1991.

facts.fact: The Victorian Robb's Buildings were demolished for the scheme, cut from three towers to two.
facts.quote: Grocon successfully argued that Robb's Building stood in the way of its major three-tower proposal, which they modified to a two-tower proposal, but still demolished the Robbs building.

facts.fact: The rear wings of the historic Rialto and Winfield buildings became a hotel around a new atrium.
facts.quote: A hotel was created utilising the whole of the long rear wing of the Rialto Building, the replacement of the rear wing of the Winfield Building, and the creation of an atrium between.

facts.fact: It had Melbourne's first public observation deck in a skyscraper, open from 1994 to 2009.
facts.quote: The Rialto featured Melbourne's first skyscraper public observation deck, which operated between 1994 and 31 December 2009.

facts.fact: Te Uru Waitākere Contemporary Gallery, formerly Lopdell House Gallery, is a contemporary art gallery in Titirangi, Auckland.
facts.quote: Te Uru Waitākere Contemporary Gallery (commonly known as Te Uru, formerly known as Lopdell House Gallery) is a contemporary art gallery located in Titirangi, Auckland.

facts.fact: The gallery serves West Auckland and first opened inside Lopdell House in 1986.
facts.quote: The gallery, which serves the West Auckland region, was originally opened within Lopdell House in 1986.

facts.fact: Its new purpose-built gallery, designed by Julie Stout of Mitchell & Stout Architects, opened on 1 November 2014.
facts.quote: The gallery closed in 2012 for a building project, with the new custom-built gallery, designed by Julie Stout of Mitchell & Stout Architects, opening on 1 November 2014.

facts.fact: Stout also refurbished Lopdell House in Titirangi in 2014.
facts.quote: Lopdell House refurbishment, Titirangi (2014)

facts.fact: The building won awards at the 2015 Auckland Architecture Awards and the 2015 New Zealand Architecture Awards.
facts.quote: The building project received a warm critical reception and has received awards in the 2015 Auckland Architecture Awards Public Building and Heritage categories, and the 2015 New Zealand Architecture Awards Public Building category.

facts.fact: Its name comes from Te Hau a Uru, 'wind from the west', and was chosen with local iwi Te Kawerau ā Maki.
facts.quote: The name of the gallery references the Māori phrase Te Hau a Uru (wind from the west), meaning the air currents the West Auckland (Waitākere/Hikurangi) area is known for. The name was chosen in consultation with local iwi Te Kawerau ā Maki.

facts.fact: It hosts the Portage Ceramic Awards, New Zealand's premier ceramics prize.
facts.quote: Te Uru hosts the annual Portage Ceramic Awards, New Zealand's premier prize for ceramics.

facts.fact: Sydney Tower, long known as Centrepoint Tower, is an observation and telecommunications tower and the tallest structure in Sydney.
facts.quote: Sydney Tower, also known as the Sydney Tower Eye, Westfield Tower and formerly albeit still commonly as Centrepoint Tower, is an observation and telecommunications tower that is the tallest structure in Sydney, New South Wales, Australia, as well as the second-tallest observation tower in the Southern Hemisphere.

facts.fact: It rises 309 metres over the CBD on Market Street, between Pitt and Castlereagh Streets.
facts.quote: The tower stands 309 m (1,014 ft) above the Sydney central business district (CBD), located on Market Street, between Pitt and Castlereagh Streets.

facts.fact: It sits on top of the Westfield Sydney (formerly Centrepoint) shopping centre.
facts.quote: It is accessible from the Pitt Street Mall, Market Street or Castlereagh Street and sits above the Westfield Sydney (formerly Centrepoint) shopping centre.

facts.fact: Designed by Donald Crone, it was first shown in plans in March 1968; tower construction began in 1975.
facts.quote: Designed by Australian architect Donald Crone, the first plans for Sydney Tower were unveiled in March 1968. Construction of the office building started in 1970, and tower construction began in 1975.

facts.fact: It opened to the public on 25 September 1981.
facts.quote: Public access to the tower began on 25 September 1981.

facts.fact: The golden turret near the top holds up to 960 people.
facts.quote: The golden turret near the top of the tower has a maximum capacity of 960 people.

facts.fact: Its lifts run at full, half or quarter speed depending on the wind.
facts.quote: The lifts travel at full, half or quarter speed, depending on wind conditions.

facts.fact: It received an Engineering Heritage Plaque from Engineers Australia.
facts.quote: The tower received an Engineering Heritage Plaque from Engineers Australia as part of its Engineering Heritage Recognition Program.

facts.fact: Southern Cross, called Spencer Street station until 2005, is a major railway station at the western edge of Melbourne's CBD.
facts.quote: Southern Cross station (known as Spencer Street station until 2005) is a major railway station in Docklands, Melbourne. It is on Spencer Street, between Collins and La Trobe streets, at the western edge of the Melbourne central business district.

facts.fact: It is the terminus of Victoria's regional rail network and of trains to Adelaide and Sydney.
facts.quote: The station is the terminus of the state's regional railway network, operated by V/Line, The Overland rail service to Adelaide, and NSW TrainLink XPT services to Sydney.

facts.fact: The station first opened as Spencer Street in 1859.
facts.quote: Opened as Spencer Street station in 1859, five years after the other major Melbourne rail terminus at Flinders Street, the station was a dead-end terminus, running parallel to Spencer Street, composed of a single main platform with a dock platform at the north end.

facts.fact: It was rebuilt to a design by Grimshaw Architects and Jackson Architecture with an undulating roof, between October 2002 and late 2006.
facts.quote: Southern Cross was redeveloped by the Civic Nexus consortium, following an innovative design by Grimshaw Architects and Jackson Architecture which features an undulating roof. Construction began in October 2002 and was completed in late 2006, with the majority of the transport facilities finished in time for the 2006 Commonwealth Games.

facts.fact: The design's main features include the wave-shaped roof, a new entrance and concourse on Collins Street and a new coach interchange.
facts.quote: The central features of the design include a wave-shaped roof, a new entrance and concourse on Collins Street, a new coach interchange, a new food court, a bar/restaurant, separate retail outlets inside the station and a separate shopping complex between Bourke and La Trobe streets.

facts.fact: WSP Global did the structural engineering.
facts.quote: The structural engineering design was performed by WSP Global.

facts.fact: It won the RIBA Lubetkin Prize for the most outstanding building outside the European Union.
facts.quote: The station has been awarded the Royal Institute of British Architects' Lubetkin Prize for most outstanding building outside the European Union.

facts.fact: Local architects criticise its poor connection to the streets around it.
facts.quote: Local architects have cited some of the Southern Cross station's shortcomings: the building's poor connection to the surrounding streets; its awkward juncture at the pedestrian bridge that links Spencer Street to Docklands Stadium; and the baffling manner in which the grand architectural gesture of Southern Cross Station tapers off into an uninspired homage to the boxy 1980s shopping centre—Spencer Outlet Centre.

facts.fact: The University of Warsaw Library (BUW) serves the University of Warsaw.
facts.quote: The University of Warsaw Library (Polish: Biblioteka Uniwersytecka w Warszawie, BUW) is a library of the University of Warsaw, Poland.

facts.fact: Its new building, by Marek Budzyński and Zbigniew Badowski, was chosen in the 1990s and opened on 15 December 1999.
facts.quote: A design by architects Marek Budzyński and Zbigniew Badowski was chosen, and the new library building was opened on 15 December 1999.

facts.fact: Pope John Paul II blessed the building on 11 June 1999.
facts.quote: Six months before, on 11 June 1999, the building was blessed by Pope John Paul II.

facts.fact: The building has a botanical garden on its roof, designed by Irena Bajerska, among the largest in Europe and open to the public.
facts.quote: The library's building includes a botanical garden on its roof, designed by Irena Bajerska, which is among the largest in Europe and open to the public.

facts.fact: The roof garden covers one hectare.
facts.quote: The distinct new building includes a botanical garden, located on the roof. The garden designed by landscape architect Irena Bajerska, has an area of one hectare, and is one of the largest roof gardens in Europe.

facts.fact: The upper garden is split into four: Golden to the north, Silver to the east, Crimson to the south and Green to the west.
facts.quote: The upper part of the garden consists of four parts: the Golden Garden (to the north), the Silver Garden (to the east), the Crimson Garden (to the south) and the Green Garden (to the west).

facts.fact: The main facade on Dobra Street carries large blocks of classical texts in different scripts, including Kochanowski in Old Polish, Plato in Greek and Ezekiel in Hebrew.
facts.quote: The main facade on the Dobra Street side contains large blocks of classical texts in various scripts, including the Old Polish text of Jan Kochanowski, Classical Greek text by Plato and Hebrew script from the Book of Ezekiel.

facts.fact: The library holds a traditional Japanese tea pavilion, Chashitsu, given by Kyoei Steel in 2004.
facts.quote: The library also houses a traditional Japanese tea pavilion, Chashitsu, donated by Kyoei Steel in 2004 and used for events related to Japanese tea culture.

facts.fact: Legiobanka, the Bank of the Czechoslovak Legions, was a cooperative bank founded in Irkutsk in 1919 to serve the Czechoslovak Legion.
facts.quote: The Bank of the Czechoslovak Legions (Czech: Banka československých legií), generally referred to as Legiobanka, was a cooperative bank in interwar Czechoslovakia. It was founded in Irkutsk in 1919 to serve the financial needs of the Czechoslovak Legion and prospered in subsequent years thanks to its strong patriotic associations.

facts.fact: Josef Gočár designed its Prague head office in 1921, and the bank moved in in 1923.
facts.quote: In 1923, it moved into its own new head office building designed by architect Josef Gočár in 1921.

facts.fact: The building so typifies rondocubism, the Czechoslovak version of art deco, that the style is sometimes called the Legiobanka style.
facts.quote: Its head office building in Prague, designed by Josef Gočár, is so representative of the particular Czechoslovak version of art deco architecture known as rondocubism that the latter is sometimes referred to as Legiobanka style (sometimes "Legiobank style").

facts.fact: Gočár moved from cubism to the 'national' Czech Rondocubism style in the early 1920s.
facts.quote: After his involvement in cubism, Gočár turned to "national" Czech Rondocubism style in the early 1920s.

facts.fact: The facade carries four sculptures by Jan Štursa of the Legion's battles on the Italian, Eastern, Russian Far East and Western fronts.
facts.quote: It displays four figurative representations by sculptor Jan Štursa of the Legion's fighting, respectively on the Italian front (battles of Doss'Alto and the Piave), Eastern Front (Zborov), Russian Far East (the revolt of the Czechoslovak Legion on the Trans-Siberian Railway, known in Czech as the Magistrále), and Western Front (Vouziers and the Terron).

facts.fact: Above them, a frieze by Otto Gutfreund shows the Legions' return; František Kysela led the interior design.
facts.quote: Above these is a frieze depicting the return of the Legions, by Otto Gutfreund. Visual artist František Kysela led the interior design.

facts.fact: ČSOB bought the building in 1990 and renovated it in 1991–1994.
facts.quote: The building was purchased in 1990 by ČSOB, which had it renovated in 1991–1994 and keeps a branch at the street level.

facts.fact: With the Archa Theatre revived in 1994, the whole building is also known as the Archa Palace.
facts.quote: In 1994, the theatre was revived again as Archa Theatre, after which the entire building is also known as the Archa Palace (Czech: Palác Archa).

facts.fact: The Fairmont Golden Prague, formerly the InterContinental Prague, is a Brutalist luxury hotel by Karel Filsak, built 1968–1974 on the Vltava at the north end of Pařížská Street.
facts.quote: The Fairmont Golden Prague, formerly the InterContinental Prague, is a historic luxury hotel and Brutalist building in Prague, Czech Republic. Designed by Czech architect Karel Filsak and built between 1968 and 1974, it stands on the Vltava riverfront at the northern end of Pařížská Street.

facts.fact: It was Czechoslovakia's first international five-star hotel, developed by the state travel agency ČEDOK with InterContinental.
facts.quote: The project was developed by the state travel agency ČEDOK in cooperation with Intercontinental Hotels Corporation and became the first international five-star hotel in Czechoslovakia.

facts.fact: Architecture, interiors and art were conceived as one whole; the interiors were designed by teams under Jan Šrámek and František Cubr.
facts.quote: Its architecture, interiors and artworks were conceived as an integrated whole, with the interiors designed by teams led by Jan Šrámek and František Cubr.

facts.fact: It officially opened on 7 December 1974.
facts.quote: Trial operation began in August 1974, and the hotel officially opened on 7 December 1974.

facts.fact: Sculptor Zbyněk Sekal designed the ceramic elements of the facades.
facts.quote: Sculptor Zbyněk Sekal designed the ceramic elements of the façades, while René Roubíček, a leading figure in modern Czech glass art, created the glass lighting for the conference hall.

facts.fact: Stanislav Libenský and Jaroslava Brychtová made architectural glass works for the hotel.
facts.quote: Sculptor Hugo Demartini designed gilded light fixtures, and Stanislav Libenský and Jaroslava Brychtová, whose work was influential in the development of monumental glass sculpture, created architectural glass works for the hotel.

facts.fact: A 2020–2025 reconstruction by Marek Tichý of TaK Architects restored Filsak's exposed concrete, ceramic facade and post-war art.
facts.quote: The reconstruction was led by architect Marek Tichý of TaK Architects and sought to restore elements of Filsak's original design that had been obscured by later alterations. Exposed concrete, the ceramic façade and significant works of Czech post-war art were restored.

facts.fact: The nine-storey building reopened on 15 April 2025 as the Fairmont Golden Prague, with 320 rooms, suites and residences.
facts.quote: The building underwent an extensive reconstruction between 2021 and 2025 and reopened on 15 April 2025 as the Fairmont Golden Prague, operated by Fairmont Hotels and Resorts. The nine-storey building comprises 320 rooms, suites and serviced residences.

facts.fact: The Hôtel de Ville is Le Havre's city hall, listed as a monument historique in 2017.
facts.quote: The Hôtel de Ville (French pronunciation: [otɛl də vil], City Hall) is the local seat of government in Le Havre, Normandy, France. It was designated a monument historique by the French government in 2017.

facts.fact: It replaced the 1857 town hall, destroyed by British bombing in September 1944.
facts.quote: The Hôtel de Ville was commissioned to replace a 19th-century town hall, which was designed by Charles Brunet-Debaine in the Châteauesque style, built in ashlar stone and completed in 1857. It was completely destroyed by British military bombardment in September 1944 during the Second World War.

facts.fact: Auguste Perret designed it in reinforced concrete, begun in 1953; after his death in 1954 Jacques Tournant saw it through to its opening on 14 July 1958.
facts.quote: It was designed by Auguste Perret in the modern style and construction began using reinforced concrete in 1953. After Perret died in February 1954, Jacques Tournant supervised the development of the design until the building was officially opened on 14 July 1958.

facts.fact: The symmetrical south front has 15 bays of tall windows between columns carrying a long entablature.
facts.quote: The design of the main block involved a symmetrical main frontage of 15 bays facing south onto Place d'Hôtel de Ville. It was fenestrated by tall casement windows on the first floor and by smaller casement windows on the second floor, all flanked by columns supporting a long entablature.

facts.fact: A 143-metre main block holds the reception rooms, and an 18-storey, 70-metre tower at the west end holds the offices.
facts.quote: The main block, which accommodated the exhibition and reception rooms, was 143 metres (469 ft) in length, and the 18-storey tower, at the west end, which accommodated the offices, was 70 metres (230 ft) high.

facts.fact: The tower was strongly criticised, as skyscrapers were thought American, not French.
facts.quote: The design was initially controversial, as some members of the city council wanted a reconstruction of the earlier city hall. The tower drew strong criticism, as such skyscrapers were considered American and not French.

facts.fact: Perret's rebuilt city has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005.
facts.quote: Perret's redesigned city has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005.

facts.fact: Tour Montparnasse is a 210-metre office tower in Paris, built 1969–1973, and was France's tallest skyscraper until 2011.
facts.quote: Tour Maine-Montparnasse (Maine-Montparnasse Tower), also commonly named Tour Montparnasse, is a 210-metre (689 ft) office skyscraper in the Montparnasse area of Paris, France. Constructed from 1969 to 1973, it was the tallest skyscraper in France until 2011, when it was surpassed by the 231-metre (758 ft) Tour First in the La Défense business district west of Paris's city limits.

facts.fact: It is still the tallest building within Paris proper.
facts.quote: It remains the tallest building in Paris proper and the fourth tallest in France, behind the Link, Tour First and Tour Hekla.

facts.fact: It was designed by Eugène Beaudouin, Urbain Cassan and Louis de Hoÿm de Marien.
facts.quote: The tower was designed by architects Eugène Beaudouin, Urbain Cassan, and Louis de Hoÿm de Marien and built by Campenon Bernard.

facts.fact: It has 59 floors and stands over Montparnasse–Bienvenüe Métro station.
facts.quote: The building has 59 floors and is built on top of the Montparnasse–Bienvenüe station of the Paris Métro.

facts.fact: It rests on 56 reinforced concrete piers reaching 70 metres down, with a concrete shield protecting the Métro below.
facts.quote: The foundations of the tower are made up of 56 reinforced concrete pillars sinking 70 m (230 ft) underground. For urban planning reasons, the tower had to be built just above a Metro line; and to avoid using the same support and weakening it, the Metro structures were protected by a reinforced concrete shield.

facts.fact: Only the offices around the edge of each floor have windows.
facts.quote: Only the offices around the perimeter of each floor of Tour Montparnasse have windows.

facts.fact: Criticised as out of place in Paris, it led to a ban on central buildings over seven storeys two years after completion.
facts.quote: The tower's simple architecture, large proportions and monolithic appearance have been often criticised by Parisians for being out of place in Paris's cityscape. As a result, two years after its completion the construction of buildings over seven storeys tall in the city centre was banned in Paris.

facts.fact: In 2017 Nouvelle AOM won a competition to redesign its facade.
facts.quote: On 21 September 2017, Nouvelle AOM won a competition to redesign the building's façade.

facts.fact: Stade de France is France's national stadium, in Saint-Denis just north of Paris, and with 81,338 seats the largest in the country.
facts.quote: Stade de France (French pronunciation: [stad də fʁɑ̃s], lit. 'Stadium of France') is the national stadium of France, located just north of Paris in the commune of Saint-Denis. Its seating capacity of 81,338 makes it the largest stadium in France.

facts.fact: It was built for the 1998 FIFA World Cup, and France beat Brazil 3–0 there in the final; Michel Platini suggested its name.
facts.quote: Initially built for the 1998 FIFA World Cup and the 2008 Summer Olympics failed bid, the stadium's name was recommended by Michel Platini, head of the organizing committee. On 12 July 1998, France beat Brazil 3–0 in the 1998 FIFA World Cup final held at the stadium.

facts.fact: Construction began on 2 May 1995, with only 31 months to finish it.
facts.quote: With only 31 months to complete the stadium, construction commenced on 2 May 1995.

facts.fact: It opened on 28 January 1998 with a France–Spain friendly.
facts.quote: The stadium was inaugurated on 28 January 1998, with a friendly football match between France and Spain.

facts.fact: A movable lower stand retracts to reveal the athletics track; the rear sections drop 7.1 m and the inner sections slide 15 m back.
facts.quote: To reveal the running track and jumping pits, the rear sections are lowered 7.1 m, then the inner sections retract 15 m into the space created, carried by ten distinct elements of 700 tons each.

facts.fact: Its architecture is inspired by Pan Am's Worldport at JFK Airport, and IABSE gave it a structural prize in 2002.
facts.quote: The architecture of the Stade de France is inspired by the Worldport of the American airline Pan American at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York.
