In 2002, the International Association for Bridge and Structural Engineering (IABSE) awarded a prize recognizing the unique structure of the stadium, commenting that Stade de France exhibited "a construction of an attractive open architecture of the city, with an elegance and natural lightness".

facts.fact: The roof covers six hectares and weighs 13,000 tonnes, sheltering the spectators but not the pitch.
facts.quote: Its area of six hectares and weight, 13,000 tons, is considered a technical marvel by many. It was designed to easily protect the 80,000 spectators without covering the playing field.

facts.fact: Tinted glass at the centre of the roof filters out red and infrared light but lets through the blue and green light the grass needs.
facts.quote: The tinted glass in the center reduces the contrast and distributes natural light. It filters out red and infrared radiation, but lets through blue and green light, due to their necessity in the health of the turf.

facts.fact: The Palais de Chaillot stands on the Chaillot Hill at the Trocadéro, in the 16th arrondissement of Paris.
facts.quote: The Chaillot Palace ( shah-YOH; French: Palais de Chaillot [palɛ də ʃajo]) is a building atop the Chaillot Hill in the Trocadéro area, in the 16th arrondissement of Paris, France.

facts.fact: It was made for the 1937 Exposition Internationale by partly demolishing and partly rebuilding the 1878 Palais du Trocadéro.
facts.quote: For the Exposition Internationale of 1937, the old 1878 Palais du Trocadéro was partly demolished and partly rebuilt to create the Chaillot Palace.

facts.fact: Louis-Hippolyte Boileau, Jacques Carlu and Léon Azéma designed it in a classicising 'moderne' style.
facts.quote: The building was designed in classicising "moderne" style by architects Louis-Hippolyte Boileau, Jacques Carlu and Léon Azéma.

facts.fact: Two curved wings, the old palace's wings with new taller fronts, form a wide arc.
facts.quote: The Palace consists of two separate wings shaped to form a wide arc, which are those of the former Palais du Trocadéro with new taller portions built in front.

facts.fact: The old central hall and towers were removed, leaving a wide esplanade with an open view to the Eiffel Tower.
facts.quote: The large central hall and towers of the old palace were demolished, leaving only the basement, with a wide esplanade created on top, establishing an open view from the Place du Trocadéro to the Eiffel Tower and beyond.

facts.fact: The buildings carry quotations by Paul Valéry and sculpture groups by Delamarre, Sarrabezolles and Bottiau.
facts.quote: The buildings are decorated with quotations by Paul Valéry, and sculptural groups at the attic level by Raymond Delamarre, Carlo Sarrabezolles and Alfred Bottiau.

facts.fact: Its eastern wing houses the Cité de l'Architecture et du Patrimoine and leads to the Théâtre national de Chaillot below the esplanade.
facts.quote: the Cité de l'Architecture et du Patrimoine, including the Musée national des Monuments Français, in the eastern (Paris) wing, from which one also enters the Théâtre national de Chaillot, a theatre below the esplanade.

facts.fact: The UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights here on 10 December 1948.
facts.quote: It is in the Chaillot Palace that the UNGA adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948.

facts.fact: The Mobilier National in Paris (1937) is one of Auguste Perret's major works.
facts.quote: His major works include the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, the first Art Deco building in Paris; the Church of Notre-Dame du Raincy (1922–23); the Mobilier National in Paris (1937); and the French Economic, Social and Environmental Council building in Paris (1937–39).

facts.fact: It is the national government furniture workshop in Paris.
facts.quote: His major works included the building of the French Economic, Social and Environmental Council, originally built for the Museum of Public Works of the 1937 Paris Exposition;  and the Mobilier Nationale, the national government furniture atelier in Paris.

facts.fact: Station F is a startup incubator in the 13th arrondissement of Paris, near the Bibliothèque nationale de France, and is said to be the world's largest startup facility.
facts.quote: Station F is a business incubator for startups, located in the 13th arrondissement, Paris, near the François Mitterrand site of the Bibliothèque nationale de France. It is noted as the world's largest startup facility.

facts.fact: The Halle Freyssinet, the messengers' hall of the Gare d'Austerlitz, was built in 1927–1929.
facts.quote: 1927-1929: the Halle Freyssinet or Halle messengers of the Gare d'Austerlitz in Paris

facts.fact: Its engineer, Eugène Freyssinet, was the major pioneer of prestressed concrete.
facts.quote: Eugène Freyssinet (French: [øʒɛn fʁɛsinɛ]) (13 July 1879 – 8 June 1962) was a French structural and civil engineer. He was the major pioneer of prestressed concrete.

facts.fact: The former rail depot, first opened in 1929, was extensively remodelled by Wilmotte & Associés for start-ups.
facts.quote: Station F occupies a building designed by French engineer Eugène Freyssinet. First opened in 1929, the former rail depot has been extensively remodeled by architects Wilmotte and Associates to meet the needs of small start-up companies.

facts.fact: The 34,000 m² facility, named F for Freyssinet, was opened by President Emmanuel Macron in June 2017.
facts.quote: Situated in a former rail freight depot previously known as la Halle Freyssinet (thereof the "F" in Station F), the 34,000 m2 (370,000 sq ft) facility was formally opened by President Emmanuel Macron in June 2017 and provides office accommodation for up to 1,000 start-up and early stage businesses as well as for corporate partners such as Facebook, Microsoft and Naver.

facts.fact: It holds 3,000 desks, meeting rooms, a 370-seat auditorium and dining open to the public.
facts.quote: As well as 3,000 desk spaces and private meeting facilities, the incubator also hosts a 370-seat auditorium and dining facilities open to the public.

facts.fact: It also houses La Felicità, a 4,500 m² food hall said to be Europe's largest restaurant.
facts.quote: The campus also houses La Felicità, the largest restaurant in Europe, with 4,500 square meters (48,000 sq ft) from the Big Mamma restaurant group.

facts.fact: The Passerelle Simone-de-Beauvoir is a footbridge for pedestrians and cyclists over the Seine in Paris, the city's 37th bridge on the river.
facts.quote: The Passerelle Simone-de-Beauvoir (French pronunciation: [pasʁɛl simɔn də bovwaʁ]; initially known by the provisional name of passerelle Bercy-Tolbiac) is a bridge solely for pedestrians and cyclists across the Seine River in Paris. It is the 37th bridge on the Seine in Paris.

facts.fact: Dietmar Feichtinger won the competition for it in 1998; it is 304 metres long with a 190-metre clear span, and the first Paris bridge named after a woman.
facts.quote: In 1998, he won the competition for the Passerelle Simone-de-Beauvoir over the Seine, facing the Bibliothèque Nationale de France. Inaugurated by Bertrand Delanoë on 13 July 2006, the bridge has a total length of 304 meters and a clear span of 190 meters and is the first of the 37 Parisian bridges to carry the name of a female personality.

facts.fact: It lies between the Pont de Bercy and the Pont de Tolbiac, linking the 12th and 13th arrondissements.
facts.quote: It is located between the bridges of Pont de Bercy and Pont de Tolbiac and links up the 12th and 13th arrondissements of Paris.

facts.fact: Its steel central span, the 'lens', weighs 650 tonnes and is 106 metres long and 12 metres wide.
facts.quote: The central span of the bridge (named the peltinée by its architects, Feichtinger Architectes, under Dietmar Feichtinger) is made of steel, weighs 650 tonnes (640 long tons; 720 short tons), is 106 metres (348 ft) long and 12 metres (39 ft) wide.

facts.fact: It is a lens-shaped structure whose geometry reduces shear.
facts.quote: The geometry of its members reduces shearing. This is a lens-shaped structure.

facts.fact: Its five crossings span the river with no supports in the water.
facts.quote: Its five crossings pass over the river without supports in water.

facts.fact: A sheltered area in the middle of the lens lets walkers keep out of the rain.
facts.quote: A protected area mid-way at the central lens allows pedestrians to shelter from rain.

facts.fact: Built by the Eiffel company in Alsace, the span was carried by water to Paris and lifted into place in two hours on 29 January 2006.
facts.quote: The span was constructed by the Eiffel company (Eiffel Constructions métalliques) in the Alsace and was transported by canal, the North Sea, the English Channel and French rivers (with difficulties due to sluices being too narrow) to its destination, crossing Paris on a barge on 30 November 2005. It was hoisted in place in two hours on 29 January 2006, around three o'clock in the morning.

facts.fact: Tony Garnier, a French architect and city planner, worked mostly in his home city of Lyon, where he designed the Halle Tony Garnier.
facts.quote: Tony Garnier (13 August 1869 – 19 January 1948) was a noted French architect and city planner. He was most active in his home city of Lyon, where he notably designed the Halle Tony Garnier and Stade de Gerland.

facts.fact: Back in Lyon in 1904, Garnier was commissioned for a livestock market and slaughterhouse (1906–1924), later named the Halle Tony Garnier.
facts.quote: In 1904, Garnier returned to Lyon, where he received a commission for a livestock market and slaughterhouse (1906–1924), later named Halle Tony Garnier.

facts.fact: The former slaughterhouse and stockyard is now a music venue.
facts.quote: Slaughterhouse and Stockyard, later named after him Halle Tony Garnier, Lyon, 1905–1924 (now a music venue, where coincidentally another Tony Garnier performed in 2010 as part of Bob Dylan's band)

facts.fact: The Hôtel du Département des Bouches-du-Rhône, known as Le Grand Bleu, holds the headquarters and council chambers of the Bouches-du-Rhône department in Marseille.
facts.quote: The Hôtel du département des Bouches-du-Rhône, known as Le Grand Bleu, is the headquarters and council chambers of the Conseil General of Bouches-du-Rhône in Marseille, France.

facts.fact: Will Alsop and Jan Störmer designed it; the Stirling Prize-nominated building is known for its ultramarine colour.
facts.quote: The Sterling Prize-nominated building, noted for its distinct ultramarine colour, was designed by architects Will Alsop and Jan  Störmer as the new regional government headquarters.

facts.fact: In the Saint-Just district north of the centre, it brought the council's scattered offices onto one site.
facts.quote: Located north of Marseille's city centre, in the Saint-Just district, the High-Tech structure was designed to combine dispersed administrative functions into a single site.

facts.fact: It won an international competition launched in 1989, beating Foster + Partners in the final round, and was designed with the artist Brian Clarke, who treated the facade as a 'skin of art'.
facts.quote: The winner of an international architecture competition launched in 1989, which in its final round saw Alsop and John Lyall compete versus established architectural practice Foster + Partners, the Hôtel du département was designed with  architectural artist Brian Clarke, who conceived the colouration and treatment of the facade as a “skin of art”.

facts.fact: The largest public building put up in provincial France in the 20th century, it was built in 26 months and opened in 1994.
facts.quote: The landmark High-tech building, the largest public building to be constructed in the French provinces in the twentieth century, was built in 26 months, opening in 1994.

facts.fact: It is clad in blue glass using a ceramic glazing technique devised by Clarke, with a 1,200 m² composition by him along the west side.
facts.quote: The completed building is externally clad in blue-coloured glass, rendered through a novel technique of ceramic glazing devised by Clarke, to produce a 'skin of art' across the entire building; along the west elevation is a 1,200-square-metre (13,000 sq ft) linear composition by Clarke in bands of ceramic glaze screenprinted onto the panels of the facade.

facts.fact: The blue, close to Yves Klein blue, was the part of the design that took the architects longest to resolve.
facts.quote: The colour, which approximates Yves Klein blue,is cited by the architects as the portion of the design process that took the most time and consideration to resolve.

facts.fact: Two office blocks are linked by an atrium, with a separate debating chamber beside them; the building is known for its X-shaped concrete pilotis, cast in place.
facts.quote: The building is formed of two administrative blocks linked by an atrial space, and a separate building, the 'Deliberatif' or debating chamber, abuting onto the two blocks. The building is notable for its distinctive X-shaped concrete support columns or pilotis, cast in situ.
